subtopic_detail: Sudden refusal to use an arm after a longitudinal pull in a toddler
stem:
You are the emergency registrar seeing a 2 year old girl brought in by her father an hour after he lifted her by one hand to stop her stepping off a kerb. She cried briefly and has not used the arm since.

She is settled on her father's lap with the right arm held loosely at her side, forearm turned inwards. She reaches confidently for a sticker with her left hand and ignores it when you offer it on the right. There is no swelling, no bruising and no deformity, and she does not cry when you palpate the clavicle, humerus, forearm or wrist. She cries only when you attempt to turn the palm upwards. She is fully immunised, has no previous presentations and was born at term.

data_table.Examination: Right arm held in slight flexion and pronation, no swelling or bruising, no bony tenderness along clavicle, humerus, radius, ulna or wrist, distal pulses present, capillary refill under 2 seconds

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Perform a hyperpronation manoeuvre at the elbow and observe for return of arm use
options.rationale: A history of axial traction with the arm held pronated, no bony tenderness and pain only on supination is a bedside diagnosis, and reduction is attempted without imaging. Hyperpronation succeeds more often than supination flexion and is less painful, with arm use typically returning within thirty minutes. (Source: RCH CPG: Radial head subluxation)

options.text: Request radiographs of the elbow and forearm before attempting any reduction manoeuvre
options.rationale: Radiographs are reserved for an atypical history, focal bony tenderness, swelling or deformity, or failure of two reduction attempts, none of which are present. Films in this setting are usually normal and delay a manoeuvre that is both diagnostic and therapeutic. (Source: RCH CPG: Radial head subluxation)

options.text: Apply a broad arm sling and arrange fracture clinic review within the following week
options.rationale: Immobilisation treats a fracture, and this presentation has no bony tenderness, swelling or deformity to support one. A week in a sling leaves a readily reducible annular ligament entrapment untreated and prolongs the disuse. (Source: RCH CPG: Radial head subluxation)

options.text: Arrange a skeletal survey and notify child protection given the injury mechanism described
options.rationale: The mechanism given accounts fully for the presentation and matches the child's stage of development, so this is not an unexplained injury. Traction on an extended arm is the ordinary cause and a survey exposes the child to radiation without changing management. (Source: RCH CPG: Child abuse)

options.text: Give oral ibuprofen and review in four hours to see whether arm use returns spontaneously
options.rationale: Spontaneous resolution does occur but is unpredictable and leaves the child in pain and functionally one handed meanwhile. Analgesia is reasonable adjunctive care yet it is not the treatment when a simple manoeuvre resolves the problem in minutes. (Source: RCH CPG: Radial head subluxation)

explanation.summary: Radial head subluxation follows sudden longitudinal traction on a pronated extended arm and results from the annular ligament slipping over the radial head. The child holds the limb pronated and slightly flexed, refuses to use it, and is characteristically comfortable at rest with no swelling, no bruising and no bony tenderness anywhere along the limb. Pain reproduced only on attempted supination is the discriminating finding and separates it from a fracture. Reduction is attempted on clinical grounds alone, with hyperpronation preferred over supination flexion because it succeeds more often and hurts less. Radiographs belong to children with focal tenderness, swelling, deformity, an inconsistent history, or failure of two reduction attempts.
key_points: Axial traction on a pronated arm is the mechanism, most often between one and four years
Absence of swelling, bruising and bony tenderness argues strongly against fracture
Hyperpronation has a higher success rate and causes less pain than supination flexion
Arm use usually returns within thirty minutes of successful reduction
Image only for atypical history, focal bony signs, or two failed attempts
explanation.pearls: Distract the child with a sticker or toy held at the midline after the manoeuvre, because spontaneous reach across with the affected hand within thirty minutes is the most reliable confirmation of success, and warn parents that recurrence happens in about a quarter of children before the annular ligament strengthens at around five years.

subtopic_detail: Persistent moist umbilical lesion after cord separation in a well infant
stem:
You are the general practice registrar seeing a 5 week old boy whose mother reports the belly button has stayed wet since the cord came away at day twelve. She has been dabbing it with cooled boiled water and finds a small yellow stain on his singlet each day.

He is breastfeeding well, has regained above birth weight and is tracking along the 50th centile. At the umbilicus there is a pink moist stalk about 4 mm across sitting within the umbilical ring, with no surrounding redness or induration of the abdominal wall and no discharge that smells of urine or faeces. Pressing gently around the umbilicus does not cause him to cry.

data_table.Examination: Pink moist stalk 4 mm at the umbilicus within the ring, scant serous discharge, no periumbilical erythema, no induration, abdomen soft, no palpable mass

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Advise salt application by the parents twice daily and reassess the umbilicus after four weeks
options.rationale: Topical salt has been described and is sometimes used, but it is slower and less reliable than cautery performed in the clinic and depends heavily on parental technique. It is a reasonable fallback where cautery is unavailable rather than the first choice. (Source: RCH CPG: Umbilical granuloma)

options.text: Apply silver nitrate to the lesion with protection of the surrounding skin and review in one week
options.rationale: A small pink moist stalk of granulation tissue persisting after cord separation in an otherwise well infant responds to chemical cautery, and one or two applications are usually sufficient. Surrounding skin is protected with a barrier because silver nitrate causes chemical burns to normal epidermis. (Source: RCH CPG: Umbilical granuloma)

options.text: Take a swab and start oral flucloxacillin for presumed umbilical infection of the cord stump
options.rationale: Omphalitis presents with periumbilical erythema, induration, tenderness and systemic upset, none of which are present here. Treating a bloodless granulation stalk with antibiotics exposes the infant to adverse effects without addressing the tissue that is weeping. (Source: RCH CPG: Umbilical granuloma)

options.text: Arrange an abdominal ultrasound scan to define the anatomy before any local treatment is given
options.rationale: Imaging is indicated when the discharge is urinary or faecal, when the lesion is large or firm and bright red, or when granulation fails to settle after cautery, since those suggest a patent urachus or vitellointestinal remnant. Scanning every moist umbilicus adds cost and delay without altering the usual outcome. (Source: RCH CPG: Umbilical granuloma)

options.text: Refer to paediatric surgery for elective excision of the lesion under general anaesthetic
options.rationale: Surgical excision is held back for lesions that persist after adequate chemical cautery or that prove to be an umbilical polyp of intestinal or urothelial mucosa. Committing a well 5 week old to general anaesthesia ahead of a bedside treatment is disproportionate. (Source: RCH CPG: Umbilical granuloma)

explanation.summary: Granulation tissue at the umbilicus is common after cord separation and presents as a small pink moist stalk that weeps serous fluid onto clothing. The critical distinction is from an umbilical polyp, which is a remnant of the vitellointestinal duct or urachus lined by intestinal or urothelial mucosa, and from a patent urachus or vitelline duct, which discharge urine or faecal material. A polyp is typically firmer, brighter red and does not shrink with cautery, and it needs surgical referral and imaging. Omphalitis is a separate and urgent diagnosis marked by periumbilical erythema, induration and systemic illness in a neonate. Simple granulation tissue is treated with silver nitrate applied to the lesion with the surrounding skin protected, usually with resolution after one or two applications.
key_points: Granulation tissue is soft, pink and shrinks with silver nitrate; a polyp is firm, bright red and does not
Urine or faecal discharge points to a patent urachus or vitellointestinal duct and needs imaging
Periumbilical erythema and induration in a neonate indicates omphalitis and warrants urgent assessment
Protect surrounding skin during cautery because silver nitrate burns normal epidermis
Persistent lesion after adequate cautery earns a surgical opinion
explanation.pearls: Failure of a supposed granuloma to shrink after two silver nitrate applications is the practical trigger to refer, because an umbilical polyp of retained vitellointestinal mucosa will not respond to cautery and may sit above a persistent duct that requires excision.

subtopic_detail: Persistent head turn preference with a neck lump in a young infant
stem:
You are the paediatric registrar reviewing an 8 week old girl referred by her maternal child health nurse because she always turns her head one way. She was born at term by vacuum extraction after a prolonged second stage.

Her mother says she feels a firm oval lump about the size of an olive low in the right side of the neck. The head rests tilted towards the right shoulder with the chin pointing left, and you can passively rotate the chin to the right only about halfway before firm resistance. The right sternocleidomastoid is thickened and firm without warmth or overlying redness. She fixes and follows across the midline with both eyes, and her hips abduct fully and symmetrically with no clunk.

data_table.Examination: Head tilt to the right with chin rotation to the left, firm 2 cm mass within the right sternocleidomastoid, passive chin rotation to the right restricted to approximately 45 degrees, no lymphadenopathy, red reflex present bilaterally, hips stable with full symmetrical abduction

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Arrange a magnetic resonance scan of the brain and cervical cord to exclude a posterior fossa lesion
options.rationale: Neuroimaging is reserved for torticollis with neurological signs, abnormal tone, vomiting or a tilt appearing after a period of normal head control. This infant has an identifiable muscular cause and a normal neurological examination. (Source: RCH CPG: Torticollis)

options.text: Reassure the mother that the posture resolves spontaneously and review at the twelve month check
options.rationale: Watchful waiting without stretching risks progressive muscle shortening, secondary skull asymmetry and facial deformity, and children referred late have worse outcomes. Reassurance alone is appropriate only for positional preference without restriction or a mass. (Source: RCH CPG: Torticollis)

options.text: Refer for physiotherapy with a home stretching and positioning programme and arrange clinical review
options.rationale: Restricted passive rotation with a firm mass within the sternocleidomastoid after an instrumental birth is the typical picture, and early physiotherapy with stretching and positioning resolves the great majority when started in the first months. Earlier referral gives better outcomes, so the programme begins now rather than after further investigation. (Source: RCH CPG: Torticollis)

options.text: Arrange urgent ultrasound of the neck mass and cervical spine radiographs before any treatment
options.rationale: Ultrasound is used when the mass has atypical features or the diagnosis is unclear, and radiographs when a bony anomaly of the cervical spine is suspected. A firm mass confined to the sternocleidomastoid with the classic tilt and rotation pattern needs neither before starting stretches. (Source: RCH CPG: Torticollis)

options.text: Refer to ophthalmology for assessment of an ocular cause of the persistent head posture
options.rationale: Ocular torticollis from a superior oblique palsy is a genuine cause of head tilt but produces no neck mass and no restriction of passive rotation. It also tends to appear once fixation matures rather than in the first weeks. (Source: RCH CPG: Torticollis)

explanation.summary: Congenital muscular torticollis is the commonest cause of a fixed head tilt in early infancy and is associated with difficult or instrumental delivery and intrauterine crowding. The head tilts towards the affected sternocleidomastoid and the chin rotates away from it, and a firm fusiform mass within the muscle is present in a proportion of infants. Restriction of passive rotation is what separates it from a simple positional preference and from ocular torticollis, in which passive range is full. Management is physiotherapy with a stretching and positioning programme, and outcomes are best when this starts within the first few months. Imaging and specialist referral are for atypical features, neurological signs, failure to improve, or a tilt of later onset.
key_points: Head tilts towards the affected muscle and the chin rotates away from it
Restricted passive rotation distinguishes muscular from positional or ocular torticollis
Early physiotherapy resolves the large majority; late referral has poorer outcomes
Examine the hips, since developmental dysplasia coexists in a meaningful minority
Later onset tilt, vomiting or abnormal tone shifts the differential towards neuroimaging
explanation.pearls: Always examine the hips in an infant with congenital muscular torticollis, because developmental dysplasia of the hip coexists in roughly one in five and both conditions share the crowded intrauterine mechanism, so a normal neonatal hip check does not remove the need to reassess.

subtopic_detail: Progressive asymmetry of the infant skull noticed by parents at four months
stem:
You are the general practice registrar seeing a 4 month old boy whose parents are worried that the back of his head looks lopsided. They noticed it at about eight weeks and think it has become more obvious.

He sleeps on his back and spends much of the day in a car capsule that they carry between the house and the car. Viewed from above, the right occiput is flattened, the right ear sits forward of the left, and the right side of the forehead is slightly fuller than the left. The sutures feel open with no palpable ridge, and the anterior fontanelle is soft and flat. He smiles socially, follows across the midline and lifts his head well when placed on his tummy. Head circumference has tracked along the 50th centile.

data_table.Examination: Right occipital flattening with ipsilateral anterior ear displacement and ipsilateral frontal bossing, sutures palpably open with no ridging, anterior fontanelle soft and flat, full passive neck rotation both directions, head circumference on the 50th centile

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Refer urgently to neurosurgery for consideration of early suture release and cranial vault surgery
options.rationale: Surgery addresses true craniosynostosis, in which the fused suture ridges and the head shape is trapezoid with the ear pulled backwards on the affected side. The pattern here is the opposite and open sutures exclude the diagnosis. (Source: RCH CPG: Plagiocephaly)

options.text: Arrange fitting of a cranial orthotic helmet now to correct the asymmetry before growth slows further
options.rationale: Helmet therapy is considered for moderate to severe deformity that fails to improve with repositioning, usually from around six months. Fitting one before a trial of conservative measures commits the family to cost and daily wear that most infants never need. (Source: RCH CPG: Plagiocephaly)

options.text: Recommend side lying and prone sleep positions overnight to take pressure off the flattened occiput
options.rationale: Non supine sleep raises the risk of sudden unexpected death in infancy and is never advised to manage head shape. Pressure relief is achieved during waking hours and by alternating the head position within supine sleep. (Source: Red Nose Australia: Safe sleeping)

options.text: Advise repositioning with increased supervised tummy time and arrange review in six to eight weeks
options.rationale: A parallelogram head shape with the ear and forehead displaced forwards on the flattened side, open sutures and normal head growth is positional in origin and responds to repositioning and increased time off the occiput. Review confirms improvement and identifies the minority who need a helmet or further assessment. (Source: RCH CPG: Plagiocephaly)

options.text: Arrange a computed tomography scan of the skull with three dimensional reconstruction of the sutures
options.rationale: Skull imaging is directed at suspected premature suture fusion, signalled by a palpable ridge, a trapezoid rather than parallelogram shape or abnormal head growth. Scanning a typical positional deformity delivers ionising radiation to an infant brain for no change in management. (Source: RCH CPG: Plagiocephaly)

explanation.summary: Positional plagiocephaly became common after supine sleeping was adopted and is compounded by prolonged time in capsules and rockers. The characteristic shape is a parallelogram: occipital flattening with the ipsilateral ear displaced forwards and ipsilateral frontal bossing, with open sutures and normal head growth. Lambdoid craniosynostosis, the important mimic, produces a trapezoid head with the ipsilateral ear displaced backwards, a palpable ridge over the fused suture and often a compensatory mastoid bulge. Management of the positional form is repositioning, supervised tummy time while awake, and treatment of any coexisting torticollis, with review to confirm improvement. Helmet therapy is reserved for moderate or severe deformity that has not improved with these measures, and safe supine sleep is never traded away for head shape.
key_points: Parallelogram shape with the ear forwards on the flat side indicates a positional cause
Trapezoid shape with the ear backwards and a palpable ridge suggests lambdoid synostosis
Repositioning and supervised tummy time are first line and are effective in most infants
Helmets are for moderate to severe deformity persisting despite repositioning
Supine sleep is maintained regardless of head shape concerns
explanation.pearls: Check passive neck rotation in every infant with occipital flattening, because untreated congenital muscular torticollis keeps the head resting on the same point and repositioning advice will fail until the tight sternocleidomastoid is being stretched by a physiotherapy programme.

subtopic_detail: Painless fluctuating scrotal swelling present since birth in an infant
stem:
You are the general practice registrar seeing an 11 month old boy whose parents report that one side of his scrotum has been puffy since he was born. They say it looks bigger in the evening and smaller when he wakes.

He is thriving and has had no vomiting, no irritability and no change in his bowel habit. The right hemiscrotum is enlarged and non tender, the swelling transilluminates, and you can get above it with your fingers so that the cord above is normal. Both testes are palpable within the scrotum and are of equal size. The swelling does not reduce with gentle pressure and there is no palpable thickening at the external ring.

data_table.Examination: Right hemiscrotal swelling that transilluminates, non tender, upper border palpable with normal cord above, both testes descended and equal, no palpable inguinal component, abdomen soft

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Refer for surgical repair within the next few weeks given the risk of bowel becoming trapped
options.rationale: Incarceration risk belongs to an inguinal hernia, which presents as a reducible inguinal swelling that does not transilluminate and in which the upper border cannot be defined. Early operation is the rule for hernia and the exception for hydrocele. (Source: RCH CPG: Inguinal hernia)

options.text: Arrange scrotal ultrasound with Doppler to characterise the swelling and assess testicular blood flow
options.rationale: Ultrasound is used when the testis cannot be palpated, when the swelling is solid or does not transilluminate, or when torsion or a tumour is a concern. Here both testes are palpable and normal and the physical signs already define the lesion. (Source: RCH CPG: Scrotal pain and swelling)
source_refs: RCH CPG: Scrotal pain and swelling

options.text: Aspirate the fluid in clinic to relieve the swelling and to confirm the nature of the contents
options.rationale: Aspiration of a paediatric hydrocele is not performed because the fluid reaccumulates through the patent processus and the needle risks injuring bowel within a coexisting hernia. Definitive treatment when needed is ligation of the processus vaginalis. (Source: RCH CPG: Scrotal pain and swelling)
source_refs: RCH CPG: Scrotal pain and swelling

options.text: Refer urgently to the emergency department for exploration given the possibility of testicular torsion
options.rationale: Torsion presents with sudden severe pain, a tender high riding testis and an unwell child, and has a course of hours rather than eleven months. A painless swelling of this duration does not fit and urgent exploration is not warranted. (Source: RCH CPG: Scrotal pain and swelling)
source_refs: RCH CPG: Scrotal pain and swelling

options.text: Reassure the parents and review at two years of age, referring if the swelling persists then
options.rationale: A transilluminating scrotal swelling with a normal cord above it and no inguinal component is a communicating hydrocele, and the processus vaginalis closes spontaneously in most boys during the first two years. Referral is made if it persists beyond that age, enlarges progressively, or an inguinal component appears. (Source: RCH CPG: Scrotal pain and swelling)
source_refs: RCH CPG: Scrotal pain and swelling

explanation.summary: A hydrocele in an infant reflects fluid tracking down a patent processus vaginalis and characteristically transilluminates, is painless and varies in size across the day. The critical bedside distinction from an inguinal hernia is whether the upper border can be defined with a normal cord above and whether the swelling reduces, since a hernia extends into the inguinal canal, does not transilluminate reliably and can be reduced. Most communicating hydroceles resolve as the processus closes during the first two years, so observation is standard. Surgical referral follows persistence beyond two years, progressive enlargement, or the appearance of an inguinal component. Aspiration has no role in children because fluid simply reaccumulates and bowel may be injured.
key_points: Transillumination and a palpable upper border with normal cord identify a hydrocele
Failure to get above the swelling or a reducible mass indicates an inguinal hernia
Most communicating hydroceles resolve spontaneously by two years of age
Hernia in infancy is repaired promptly because of incarceration risk
Aspiration is not used in children; ligation of the processus is the operation when needed
explanation.pearls: A hydrocele that appears for the first time after infancy, or one that becomes tense and tender in an older boy, should prompt scrotal ultrasound rather than reassurance, since a reactive hydrocele can be the presenting sign of an underlying testicular tumour or of torsion of an appendix testis.

sources.label: RCH CPG: Scrotal pain and swelling
